# Contribution of Meals and Snacks Provided through the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) on Young Children’s Total Dietary Intake

**Authors:** Kelsey L. Kinderknecht; Meghan Zimmer; Rebecca Mozaffarian; Erica L. Kenney

**Affiliations:** Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts. | Departments of Nutrition and Social and Behavioral Sciences at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts.

## Abstract

Several federal food assistance programs support children’s nutrition. However, evidence is limited on how the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP), specifically, contributes to children’s dietary intake.

The study objective was to understand how CACFP meals and snacks contribute to young children’s overall dietary intake on a given day.

A within-person, observational study design was used.

Participants were one- to six-year-old children (n=1004) attending CACFP-participating early care and education (ECE) programs participating in the 2017 U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Study of Nutrition and Activity in Childcare Settings (SNACS).

Daily energy-adjusted food group/specific nutrient intakes were the primary outcome measures, standardized by kilocalories consumed.

Paired t-tests evaluated how a child’s energy-adjusted dietary intake at a CACFP-participating ECE program compared to elsewhere on the same day, and analyses were stratified by duration of attendance at an ECE program and household food security status.

Children attending an ECE program for a full day consumed most of their fruit (54%, SE: 0.02), whole grains (67%, SE: 0.03), and dairy (61%, SE: 0.02) from CACFP meals and snacks. When children ate at full day ECE programs, they consumed significantly more energy-adjusted dairy (0.3 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: 0.12, 0.40) and whole grains (0.1 oz-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.25), and less vegetables (−0.1 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.21, −0.08), protein foods (−0.4 oz-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.60, −0.26), sodium (−211 mg/1000kcals, 95% CI: −283.1, −139.8), saturated fat (−2.1 g/1000kcals, 95% CI: −2.91, −1.28), and added sugars (−6.8 g/1000kcals, 95% CI: −10.15, −3.54) than when they were not at an ECE program. Patterns in energy-adjusted intake differences remained for those experiencing food security compared to food insecurity except for whole grains; children experiencing food security had a significantly higher consumption of whole grains at a full-day ECE program compared to elsewhere (0.2 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.26) whereas there was no difference for children experiencing food insecurity.

CACFP meals and snacks support nutritious diets for young children by contributing to higher energy-adjusted intakes of dairy and whole grains, and lower energy-adjusted intakes of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars compared to what children consume elsewhere. Future research should examine how CACFP can further support nutritious diets for children.

## INTRODUCTION

Developing healthful eating habits during early childhood is important for the prevention of diet-related chronic diseases and overall child health and well-being.1–4 While the nutritional quality of children’s eating patterns has improved over the past several decades, most children still have dietary intakes that do not align closely with the recommended diet for optimal health, such as inadequate intake of whole grains, fruits, and vegetables, and excess intake of added sugars.5–9 Policies that help promote nutritious dietary intake in early care and education (ECE) programs are particularly important for supporting improved dietary intake for young children,10,11 as children consume meals and snacks while in attendance, and 59% of U.S. 3–5 year olds attend ECE programs.12 The Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) is one such program informed by policy; it is a federal nutrition assistance program in the U.S. that sets nutrition standards and provides financial reimbursements to ECE programs for meals and snacks that meet meal pattern standards established by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). CACFP served over 4.4 million children in 2024, about 80% of whom were from low-income households,13–15 which are more likely to experience food insecurity, defined as uncertain of having or unable to acquire enough food to meet the needs of all members of their household due to insufficient money or other resources for food over the past year, and have lower diet quality.16–18

However, evidence for CACFP’s impact on children’s diet quality is surprisingly sparse.19 Prior studies have had to rely on small sample sizes, lacked comparison groups, or used unreliable measures of dietary intake.20–23 Moreover, nearly all studies have been limited to assessing dietary intake at ECE only, precluding observation of whether CACFP participation changes children’s overall dietary quality. One recent study started to address this evidence gap, using a nationally representative sample of children attending CACFP programs and validated dietary assessments, finding that children’s intakes aligned more closely with the Dietary Guidelines for Americans on child care days compared to non-child care days,24 but given that non-child care days were weekend days, it is unclear whether this was due to CACFP meals and snacks being more healthful or due to intake on weekends being generally less healthful. To build on prior literature, this study aimed to first estimate how much CACFP meals/snacks contribute to overall intake of key food and nutrient groups in a given day for children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs. This study then estimated whether CACFP meals/snacks contribute relatively more to dietary quality than meals/snacks consumed outside of ECE by comparing children’s intake of key food and nutrient groups from CACFP meals and snacks with their intake during the rest of a given day, using a within-child analytic approach to minimize confounding.

## METHODS

### Data Source and Sample

Data were used from a nationally representative cross-sectional study of children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs in program year 2016–2017 from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food and Nutrition Services (FNS) sponsored Study of Nutrition and Activity in Child Care Settings (SNACS).25 SNACS study staff collected data on 1,576 children aged 1–6 years old attending a CACFP-participating ECE program with complete dietary intake data on days attending an ECE program and parental informed consent. For this analysis, children with missing parent surveys (n=524), from which necessary sociodemographic variables were measured, were excluded, as well as those where duration at childcare was not reported (n=6) (Figure 1). Children with missing data on household food security status, a key covariate in the analysis, were also excluded (n=42). The data were de-identified and no individuals on the study team had links to identifiers. The research was considered non-human subjects research according to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Institutional Review Board (IRB23–0577).

### Measures

#### Primary Outcome.

The primary outcome for this study was children’s dietary intake of complementary foods (not including infant formula and/or breastmilk), characterized by total daily food group/nutrient intakes associated with a health-promoting eating pattern that aligns with the 2015–2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans, including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy, and protein foods, and limited intakes of saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars.1,3,4 To measure 24-hour dietary intake, a trained ECE provider used a validated meal observation method provided by the SNACS study team to assess children’s dietary intake for food consumed and sourced from the ECE program;26 then, a parent/guardian used a food diary to measure children’s dietary intake for food consumed or sourced from outside the ECE program on the same day. Study staff entered dietary data into SurveyNet (version 4.2), a computerized nutrient analysis software program developed by the USDA Food Surveys Research Group,27 and then linked to the Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies (FNDDS, version 2013–2014).28 Staff used the USDA Food Patterns Equivalents Database (FPED, version 2013–2014) to calculate the food pattern equivalents, the quantity of a food component consumed using standardized units (e.g. oz-eq, c-eq) for all foods/ingredients.29 For children with 2 days of dietary intake data on a day attending an ECE program (n=86), the outcome measures were averaged across the 2 days.

#### Sociodemographic characteristics.

Parents provided information on child’s duration of attendance at an ECE program [defined as full day (>5 hours/day) or part day (1–5 hours/day)], age (1–6 years old), sex (male or female), race/ethnicity [non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, or other (including Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander)], household income, household size, number of children in the household, receipt of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) in the past 30 days (yes/no), and receipt of Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) in the past 30 days (yes/no).30,31 The parent survey collected data on risk of household food insecurity using the 2-item Hunger Vital Sign screener.32 Household food security status was dichotomized as food secure or food insecure, with risk of food insecurity operationalized as affirmative responses (‘often true’ or ‘sometimes true’) to either or both of the following statements: “within the past 12 months we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more” and “within the past 12 months the food we bought just didn’t last and we didn’t have money to get more.”32 Variables from a survey completed by the sample children’s ECE providers supplied information on whether the child attended a metropolitan area location (yes/no), type of geographic area of program where child attended (rural, small town, suburban, and urban), and whether the child attended a Head Start program (yes/no).33

### Statistical Analysis

To characterize the overall influence of CACFP on children’s total dietary intake in a given day, the proportion of children’s food group intake (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy, and protein foods) in ounce or cup equivalents, and select nutrient intakes [sodium (milligrams), saturated fat (grams), and added sugars (grams)] were calculated by location (ECE program versus elsewhere). In sensitivity analyses, we assessed for differences in dietary outcomes between children with and without parent survey data. To test whether intake from CACFP meals/snacks was of higher nutritional quality than intake outside of the ECE program, we first calculated energy-adjusted dietary intake of the same selected food and nutrient groups above, stratified by ECE and non-ECE intakes, by dividing intake of each group by kcals consumed over the entire day (ECE and non-ECE combined). We then compared these energy-adjusted intakes of key foods and nutrients between meals/snacks consumed at ECE compared to non-ECE intake on the same day using paired t-tests. We stratified by full- or part-day attendance to account for the different amount of exposure to CACFP meals and snacks (full day: >5 hours; part day: 1–5 hours). Differences by household food security status were tested in secondary analyses to examine how consumption of meals and snacks at and away from the ECE program differed for children experiencing risk of food insecurity. Two-sided alpha was set at p <0.05.

All analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.0.34 Child-level sampling weights were used to account for the multi-stage stratified sampling strategy, clustered sampling design, and non-response bias of ECE program providers and children within classrooms.25

## RESULTS

The analytic sample included 1004 children 1–6 years old who attended 242 CACFP-participating ECE programs, had complete parent surveys and dietary intake data on days the child attended an ECE program, and had complete information on risk of household food security status (Table 1). This amounted to 64% of the original full sample (Figure 1). Most study participants were from households with incomes ≤185% of the federal poverty level (59% for full day attendance, 77% for part day attendance) and not experiencing household food insecurity (83% for full day attendance, 55% for part day attendance), with a greater proportion of children who attended a part day program being food insecure, income ≤185% of the federal poverty level, and attending a Head Start center. On average, children attending full day programs consumed 1462 kcals (SE: 52) over an entire day and 603 kcals (SE: 23) while at ECE (43% of daily energy; SE: 0.01), and children attending part day programs consumed 1540 kcals (SE: 25) over an entire day and 422 kcals (SE: 35) while at ECE (28% of daily energy; SE 0.02) (Table 1 and Figure 2).

While most children consumed at least some vegetables, fruits, dairy, whole grains, and protein foods during the entire day, a few children did not (Figure 2). Among children attending a full day ECE program who consumed a nonzero amount, children, on average, consumed 54% of their total fruit intake (SE: 0.02), 67% of their total whole grain intake (SE: 0.03), 61% of their total dairy intake (SE: 0.02), 44% of their total vegetable intake (SE: 0.02), and 41% of their total protein food intake (SE: 0.03) from CACFP meals or snacks served at the ECE program (Figure 2). For dietary components to consume in moderation, on average over an entire day, children consumed 44% of their total added sugar intake (SE: 0.04), 42% of their total saturated fat intake (SE: 0.02), and 44% of their total sodium intake (SE: 0.01) from CACFP meals and snacks served at the ECE program. For part-day attendees, on average over the entire day, children consumed slightly lower proportions of total daily intake of food components and nutrients from CACFP meals and snacks (Figure 2). Supplemental Table 2 shows differences in proportions of intake between children with and without completed parent survey data.

Children attending a full day ECE program, on average, consumed significantly more energy-adjusted dairy (0.3 c-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.12, 0.40) and whole grains (0.1 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.25) and less vegetables (−0.1 c-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −0.21, −0.08), protein foods (−0.4 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −0.60, −0.26), sodium (−211 mg/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −283.1, −139.8), saturated fat (−2.1 g/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −2.91, −1.28), and added sugars (−6.8 g/1000 kcals, 95% CI: −10.15, −3.54) from CACFP meals and snacks compared to intake from all other meals and snacks consumed that day outside of the child care program (Table 3). Meanwhile, children attending a part day ECE program, on average, consumed significantly less energy-adjusted fruits, vegetables, dairy, protein, sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars from CACFP meals and snacks compared to intake from all other meals and snacks consumed that day outside of the child care program (Table 3).

In stratified analyses, all patterns of energy-adjusted differences in intake remained for children attending a full day ECE program experiencing household food security compared to food insecurity, with the exception of intake of whole grains. Children experiencing food security had a significantly higher consumption of whole grains at an ECE program compared to elsewhere (0.2 oz-eq/1000 kcals, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.26) whereas there was no difference in whole grain intake at ECE compared to elsewhere for children experiencing food insecurity (Table 4). For children attending a part day program by food security status, all patterns in energy-adjusted differences remained except for dairy. Children experiencing food security had a significantly lower consumption of dairy at an ECE program compared to elsewhere (−0.3 c-eq/1000kcals, 95% CI: −0.55, −0.05) whereas there was no difference in dairy intake at an ECE program compared to elsewhere for children experiencing food insecurity (Table 5).

## DISCUSSION

This study found that meals and snacks served at CACFP-participating ECE programs support nutritious dietary intakes for young children by contributing a greater amount of energy-adjusted whole grains and dairy intake for children attending full day ECE programs and a lesser amount of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars for children attending both full day and part day ECE programs. At the same time, however, energy-adjusted intake of vegetables was lower from CACFP meals and snacks for full day attendees, and energy-adjusted intake of fruit and vegetables was lower for part-day attendees. Lower consumption of sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars at ECE programs is particularly important, as lower intakes of these nutrients have been associated with improved cardiometabolic health.35–37 Patterns of energy-adjusted differences remained when comparing children experiencing food security to those experiencing food insecurity; however, children from households experiencing food security consumed a significantly greater amount of whole grains while at a full day ECE program compared to elsewhere, whereas there was no difference in whole grain consumption observed for children experiencing household food insecurity.

This study’s results build on prior research on the link between receiving CACFP meals and snacks and children’s dietary intake.21,22,24 A recent systematic review of studies comparing dietary intake between CACFP-participating and nonparticipating ECE programs showed limited and mixed evidence on the association of CACFP meals and snacks on children’s dietary intake, but indicated that at least some studies found CACFP participation was associated with no differences in fruit consumption, slight increases in vegetable consumption, slight increases in whole grain consumption, lower consumption of protein foods, and increases in milk consumption.19 Similarly, this study found no differences in fruit consumption, greater whole grain consumption, greater dairy consumption, and lower consumption of protein foods from CACFP meals and snacks compared to elsewhere; however, this study found slightly lower vegetable consumption for children attending full day ECE programs. On balance, however, the results suggest that CACFP meals and snacks tend to be more healthful than what is consumed outside of CACFP-participating ECE programs, particularly with regard to lower sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars. While CACFP standards at the time did not explicitly limit sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars, the program’s emphasis on serving dairy, fruits, and vegetables, and overall emphasis on supporting children’s nutrition, may have resulted in ECE programs serving fewer foods high in these nutrients relative to what children are fed in the absence of CACFP standards. Even greater energy-adjusted differences were observed for these nutrients for children attending part day programs (i.e. higher intakes of foods that should be limited consumed away from childcare than at childcare) compared to full day programs, suggesting that, if children attending part day programs had more exposure to CACFP meals and snacks in full day programs, this may be associated with lower intakes of nutrients that should be limited over the entire day.

At the same time, our results suggest CACFP could be further strengthened. Energy-adjusted vegetable intake from CACFP meals and snacks for children attending full day ECE programs was not meaningfully different than what was consumed outside of ECE programs – and all of it was low, likely due to the bitter or undesirable taste of some vegetables and less exposure and familiarity with vegetables among children.38 Meanwhile, a substantial number of children in this study never ate a whole grain throughout the course of their entire day. While CACFP’s meal pattern standards were updated in 2017,39 it is possible that these standards are not yet strong enough to meaningfully improve young children’s diets – a possibility which has been borne out by mixed evidence from several studies that have directly evaluated the standards changes.40,41 It is also possible, however, that ECE providers simply need more support for serving health-promoting, appealing foods, given they face extraordinary barriers for ECE programs to implement CACFP.42 Research should continue to explore how best to support ECE providers so that, in turn, they are best able to provide necessary nutritious and tasty foods to the children they serve.

Strengths of the study include the use of data from SNACS, a nationally representative dataset of children attending CACFP-participating ECE programs. Another strength was the use of reliable and valid methods to measure children’s dietary intake across a 24 hour period, particularly the use of meal observations while at ECE.26 Other studies attempting to measure young children’s dietary intake over a 24 hour period often only use parental-reported 24 hour recalls, which can be difficult when parents do not know what their child actually ate while at an ECE program. Using within-child analyses eliminated potential confounding from children’s individual characteristics that might influence dietary intake (e.g. age, sex, race/ethnicity) that would be inherent in a between-child analysis (i.e. where children who consume CACFP meals and snacks are compared in aggregate with children who do not). This approach also allows us to avoid comparing ECE program days to weekend days, when children’s intakes may be substantially different regardless of ECE participation, and thus allow us to better isolate CACFP’s potential impact on a given child’s diet given the available data. Limitations include missingness on the parent survey for about one third of the initial study sample that had complete dietary outcome data. When comparing dietary outcome data between groups with missing and non-missing parent survey data, there were differences between daily proportions of whole grain and dairy consumption from CACFP meals and snacks. If these differences were not due to lack of stratification on length of CACFP attendance (since this variable was not available for children without parent survey data), these differences may have contributed to a conservative estimate of the average difference in whole grain consumption and an overestimate of the average difference in dairy consumption between what is consumed at ECE program compared to elsewhere. While parent-reported food diaries have been shown to be a reliable and valid measure to collect young children’s dietary intake, there is still potential for misclassification, specifically underreport of foods/beverages consumed, although this is likely to not be differential across children.43 The majority of children only had one day of dietary intake, which could lead to measurement error. Using two different dietary data collection methods to compare dietary intakes at ECE programs (meal observation) compared to elsewhere (parent-reported food diary) could lead to misclassification; however, the misclassification would be consistent for all children. While it is a limitation that breastmilk intake was likely not captured and it is possibly part of some children’s diets in the study sample, prior research has shown that breastfeeding and infant formula consumption tapers into being such a small contribution to children’s overall diets for children 12 months and older that it would only minimally influence the estimates.44 Another limitation is the age of the SNACS-I data; at the time of analysis, results from SNACS-II had not yet been released and to our knowledge the data were not yet publicly available (initial findings were released in July 2025), so the best dataset available for the research question was SNACS-I. While CACFP’s nutrition standards were modified after these data were collected, potentially making the data outdated, research that has examined pre/post changes in CACFP menu offerings and intake have largely found only minimal changes as a result of the standards.40,41 However, future research should evaluate whether CACFP’s contributions to children’s daily intakes have changed using more updated data as it becomes available. Future research should also incorporate consistent dietary assessment methods for children with longitudinal designs, repeated measures, and comparing children attending CACFP-participating and non-participating ECE programs.

## CONCLUSION

Meals and snacks served at CACFP-participating ECE programs significantly contribute to nutritious diets for young children. To isolate the impact of CACFP on young children’s dietary intake, future research should compare dietary intake at and away from an ECE program for children who attend CACFP-participating compared to non-CACFP participating programs. Future research should also examine strategies to expand access to CACFP for ECE providers, further improve the program to support nutritious diets, and ultimately improve reach of CACFP to young children who could benefit from the meals and snacks.
